summary: A slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs numbered 2300 through 2399, with authors, dates, titles and a short note on each, written as a status report in January 1999. It marks which ones are on the standards track. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is like a table of contents for a shelf of 100 numbered books, with one line about what each book is for.

questions: which rfcs are on the standards track
what is the rfc summary document
how do i find what an rfc does
subtitle: A catalog of 100 standards and protocols from 1998, with notes on each.

tldr.problem: The Internet has grown rapidly with hundreds of RFCs defining protocols and standards, making it hard to understand what exists and what is on the standards track.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2399 provides an annotated list of all RFCs numbered 2300 through 2399, noting which ones represent standards and which are informational.
tldr.outcome: This document serves as a snapshot in time of the standards landscape as of January 1999, showing the breadth of Internet protocols from addressing to mail security.

today: RFC 2399 is a historical informational document that cataloged the standards landscape of 1998 and early 1999. It has not been updated and is preserved as a record of that period. Later RFC summary documents cover more recent ranges.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2399 is an annotated list of 100 RFCs numbered from 2300 to 2399, published in January 1999. Each entry gives the RFC number, the author, the publication date, the full title, and a brief description of the RFC's purpose.

This document is informational and does not itself define a protocol or standard. It serves as a status report, helping readers navigate the large body of standards and experimental specifications that had been published by that point in time.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is a big list of what other Internet documents do. Think of it as a menu at a restaurant that tells you what each dish is.

sections.title: Coverage and Organization
sections.content:
The document covers 100 RFCs in sequence from RFC 2300 to RFC 2399. The entries are presented in reverse numerical order starting with RFC 2399 (the summary itself) and working backward to RFC 2300.

Each entry includes the RFC number, the author's name, the publication date, and the official title. The description for each RFC is taken directly from the RFC's own abstract or status section.
sections.plainLanguage: The list starts at 2399 and goes down to 2300, so you see the newest documents first. Each one gets a short description of what it is about.

sections.title: Standards Track Identification
sections.content:
A key feature of this document is that RFCs on the standards track are marked with [STANDARDS-TRACK]. These are documents intended to become Internet standards as they progress through the standardization process.

The document notes that RFCs may be Proposed Standards, Draft Standards, or full Standards, but because the status of RFCs can change, this document only marks whether an RFC is on the track at all, not its specific level. For precise status information, the document directs readers to the current edition of the Internet Official Protocol Standards.
sections.plainLanguage: Some documents are trying to become official Internet rules. Those ones have a mark [STANDARDS-TRACK] so you know they are important. Other documents are just ideas or reports.

sections.title: Categories of Protocols
sections.content:
The 100 RFCs from 2300 to 2399 span a wide range of Internet technologies. They include protocols for email (SMTP extensions, MIME types, IMAP commands), addressing (IPv6 architecture and multicast addresses), routing (OSPF, RSVP), security (encryption, key management), streaming media (RTP payload formats, real-time protocols), and network management.

Many are standards-track documents that define core protocols such as IPv6 addressing and OSPF routing. Others are informational or experimental, exploring techniques like multicast over ATM networks or batch SMTP operations.
sections.plainLanguage: These 100 documents describe many different Internet tools: how to send email, how to find computers by address, how to route messages, how to keep secrets, and how to stream videos. Some are real rules now, and some are still experiments.

sections.title: Status and Use
sections.content:
RFC 2399 is marked as Informational, meaning it conveys information to the Internet community but does not define a protocol or standard itself. Its main purpose is documentation and reference.

This document is a historical snapshot of the standardization effort as of January 1999. Because the RFC series is a continuous stream, newer summary RFCs have been published for later number ranges, making this document most useful for understanding the standards landscape of that era.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is just a report. It does not change how the Internet works. It is helpful if you want to know what the Internet people were working on in 1998 and 1999.
